p.src: Why the Hamiltonian Cannot Stand Alone

u.src: Why the Hamiltonian Cannot Stand Alone
en: Why the Hamiltonian Cannot Stand Alone

p.src: In the toy model, space was suppressed and the basic relation was $\{Q,Q^\dagger\}=2H.$ That form is adequate when time is the only coordinate. In a relativistic theory, however, $H=P_0$ is one component of the four-momentum $P_\mu$. A Lorentz boost mixes it with $P_i$. An algebra whose right-hand side singled out $P_0$ could not transform covariantly.

In a relativistic theory, however, $H=P_0$ is one component of the four-momentum $P_\mu$. A Lorentz boost mixes it with $P_i$. An algebra whose right-hand side singled out $P_0$ could not transform covariantly.

p.src: The repair must therefore do two things at once. It must replace $H$ by all four components $P_\mu$, and it must provide indices on the left that can be matched to a Lorentz vector on the right. The massless Dirac equation supplies the needed clue: a relativistic fermion may be described by a two-component spinor, and the matrices $\sigma^\mu$ convert a vector index into a pair of spinor indices.

p.src: Massless Fermions, Helicity, and Chirality

u.src: Massless Fermions, Helicity, and Chirality
en: Massless Fermions, Helicity, and Chirality

p.src: Begin with the physical distinction between massive and massless particles. Take a massive spin-$\tfrac12$ particle moving in the direction of its spin. Because its speed is less than the speed of light, an observer may overtake it. In the new frame the momentum reverses while the spin does not, so the helicity reverses. A Lorentz-invariant massive theory must consequently contain both helicities.

p.src: No observer can overtake a massless particle. Proper Lorentz transformations cannot reverse its momentum relative to its spin, so one irreducible massless representation may carry a single helicity. A spatial rotation can turn the flight direction around, but it does not turn a right hand into a left hand.

p.src:
Replacing $H$ by $i\partial_t$ and $\mathbf p$ by $-i\nabla$ gives $i\partial_t\chi=-i\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\nabla\chi.$ Introduce $\begin{aligned}
\sigma^\mu&=(\mathbf 1,\boldsymbol{\sigma}),\\
\bar\sigma^\mu&=(\mathbf 1,-\boldsymbol{\sigma}),\\
\eta_{\mu\nu}&=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).
\end{aligned}$ Then the equation just obtained is $i\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\chi=0.$ The conjugate Weyl representation uses $\bar\sigma^\mu$. It is this conjugate representation, named $\psi_\alpha$ below, whose free equation is $i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi=0$. Proving covariance requires the spinor representation of the Lorentz group, but the important fact here is structural: the four matrices $\sigma^\mu$ join one spacetime index to two spinor indices.

p.src: The Four-Dimensional Superalgebra

u.src: The Four-Dimensional Superalgebra
en: The Four-Dimensional Superalgebra

p.src:
The odd coordinates must now transform like Weyl spinors: $\theta^\alpha=(\theta^1,\theta^2),
\qquad
\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}=(\bar\theta^{\dot1},\bar\theta^{\dot2}).$ The bar denotes complex conjugation, and the dot distinguishes the conjugate Lorentz representation. There are two complex, or four real, Grassmann components. A general even superfield $\mathcal S=\mathcal S(x^\mu,\theta^\alpha,\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha})$ therefore has a finite Grassmann expansion. Its highest monomial is $\theta^2\bar\theta^2
\equiv
(\theta^1\theta^2)(\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}),$ the product of all four independent odd coordinates. The coefficient of this monomial is commonly called the $D$-component.

p.src:
The supercharges also carry spinor indices. In four-dimensional $N=1$ supersymmetry their algebra is $\begin{aligned}
\{Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}
&=2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu,
\\
\{Q_\alpha,Q_\beta\}&=0,
&
\{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha},\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}&=0,
\\
[P_\mu,Q_\alpha]&=0,
&
[P_\mu,\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}]&=0,
&
[P_\mu,P_\nu]&=0.
\end{aligned}$ The factor of two is conventional. The matrix $\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}$ contracts the vector index on $P_\mu$ and leaves precisely the two spinor indices appearing on the left.

p.src: A Constraint That Survives Supersymmetry

u.src: A Constraint That Survives Supersymmetry
en: A Constraint That Survives Supersymmetry

p.src: A general superfield contains many components. We seek a smaller class without destroying the symmetry. The lecture first gives an ordinary analogy. For a vector $\mathbf V$, the constraint $V_x=0$ is not rotationally invariant: after a rotation, $V_y$ contributes to the new $x$-component. By contrast, $\mathbf V^2=1$ is invariant and removes one independent degree of freedom. A useful constraint must map constrained fields into constrained fields under the symmetry.

p.src: Suppose a linear odd operator $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}$ defines $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\Phi=0.$ After a supersymmetry variation $\delta\Phi=Q\Phi$, the same condition will hold if $\bar D$ anticommutes with the supercharges: $\bar D(Q\Phi)=-Q(\bar D\Phi)=0.$ This is the abstract consistency test that motivates the construction, rather than a definition appearing without explanation.

p.src: Solving the Chiral Constraint

u.src: Solving the Chiral Constraint
en: Solving the Chiral Constraint

p.src: Define the shifted coordinate $y^\mu=x^\mu+i\theta\sigma^\mu\bar\theta.$ With the left-derivative convention above, a function $\Phi=\Phi(y,\theta)$ obeys $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\Phi=0$. The chain rule makes the cancellation explicit. Differentiating through $y^\mu$ gives the same $i\theta\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\Phi$ term that appears with the opposite sign in $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}$.

p.src:
Thus a chiral superfield has no independent $\bar\theta$-dependence. It may still contain $\bar\theta$, but only through the combination $y^\mu$. Its finite expansion is $\Phi(y,\theta)
=\phi(y)+\sqrt2\,\theta\psi(y)+\theta^2F(y).$ The three component types are a complex scalar $\phi$, a Weyl fermion $\psi_\alpha$, and a complex scalar $F$. The last is auxiliary rather than a second propagating boson.

p.src:
Expanding Eq.  at fixed $x$ gives $\begin{aligned}
\Phi(x,\theta,\bar\theta)
={}&\phi
+\sqrt2\,\theta\psi
+\theta^2F
+i\theta\sigma^\mu\bar\theta\,\partial_\mu\phi
\notag\\
&-\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\theta^2
\partial_\mu\psi\,\sigma^\mu\bar\theta
+\frac14\theta^2\bar\theta^2\Box\phi.
\end{aligned}$ All component fields on the right are evaluated at $x$. The conjugate antichiral field depends on $\bar y^\mu=x^\mu-i\theta\sigma^\mu\bar\theta$ and $\bar\theta$. A chiral superfield cannot consistently be real, because its conjugate satisfies the opposite chirality constraint.

p.src: A full-superspace action has the form $S_D=\int d^4x\,d^2\theta\,d^2\bar\theta\;K,$ where $K$ is a real superfield. Berezin integration selects its $\theta^2\bar\theta^2$ coefficient. After the odd integrations, only an ordinary spacetime Lagrangian remains.

p.src: The Free Chiral Multiplet

u.src: The Free Chiral Multiplet
en: The Free Chiral Multiplet

p.src:
This is where the derivatives come from. The superspace expression $\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ contains no explicit spacetime derivative, yet the shifted arguments generate first and second derivatives of the component fields. Multiplying the expansions and retaining only the top component gives, in the convention of Eq. , $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{free}}
=\partial_\mu\phi^\ast\partial^\mu\phi
+i\bar\psi\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi
+F^\ast F.$ Up to integration by parts, the scalar piece may instead be written schematically as $-\phi^\ast\Box\phi$, which is the form approached in the board calculation.

p.src: The Quadratic Superpotential and Equal Masses

u.src: The Quadratic Superpotential and Equal Masses
en: The Quadratic Superpotential and Equal Masses

p.src:
Propagation came from a $D$-term. Mass comes from the chiral integral. Choose the conventional normalization $W_2(\Phi)=\frac12m\Phi^2.$ The $\theta^2$ component is $\left.W_2(\Phi)\right|_{\theta^2}
=m\phi F-\frac12m\psi\psi.$ Together with the conjugate term, the component Lagrangian becomes $\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L
={}&
\partial_\mu\phi^\ast\partial^\mu\phi
+i\bar\psi\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi
+F^\ast F
\notag\\
&+m\phi F+m^\ast\phi^\ast F^\ast
-\frac12m\psi\psi
-\frac12m^\ast\bar\psi\bar\psi.
\end{aligned}$ The fermion bilinear is a Majorana mass for the Weyl field. The $F$-equations are algebraic: $F^\ast=-m\phi,
\qquad
F=-m^\ast\phi^\ast.$ Substitution gives $\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{on\ shell}}={}&
\partial_\mu\phi^\ast\partial^\mu\phi
+i\bar\psi\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi\\
&-|m|^2|\phi|^2\\
&-\frac12\left(m\psi\psi+m^\ast\bar\psi\bar\psi\right).
\end{aligned}$ Thus the scalar mass and fermion mass are both $|m|$. In the board’s diagrammatic language, a scalar turns locally into $F$ through one $m\phi F$ insertion and immediately turns back through its conjugate. Two insertions supply $|m|^2|\phi|^2$, exactly the scalar mass term found by solving Eq. .

p.src: The Cubic Superpotential and Interactions

u.src: The Cubic Superpotential and Interactions
en: The Cubic Superpotential and Interactions

p.src:
Now add $W(\Phi)=\frac12m\Phi^2+\frac13g\Phi^3.$ For a general holomorphic $W$, the $F$-component is $\left.W(\Phi)\right|_{\theta^2}
=F W'(\phi)-\frac12W''(\phi)\psi\psi.$ Here $W'(\phi)=m\phi+g\phi^2,
\qquad
W''(\phi)=m+2g\phi.$ Before eliminating $F$, the cubic term contains $g\phi^2F-g\phi\psi\psi+\text{h.c.}$ The second term is a Yukawa vertex joining one scalar to two fermion lines. The first joins two scalars to an auxiliary line.

p.src: Pedagogical redraw of the Yukawa interaction: two fermionic legs and one scalar leg meet with coupling proportional to $g$.

u.src: Pedagogical redraw of the Yukawa interaction: two fermionic legs and one scalar leg meet with coupling proportional to $g$.

caption.en: Pedagogical redraw of the Yukawa interaction: two fermionic legs and one scalar leg meet with coupling proportional to $g$.

p.src:
The complete auxiliary-field equation is $F^\ast=-W'(\phi)=-(m\phi+g\phi^2).$ Eliminating it produces the scalar potential $V(\phi)=|W'(\phi)|^2
=|m\phi+g\phi^2|^2.$ Besides the mass term, this contains cubic scalar terms proportional to $m^\ast g$ and a quartic term $V(\phi)\supset |g|^2|\phi|^4.$ In the auxiliary-line picture, two $\phi^2F$ vertices are connected by the local $F$-contraction. Because Eq.  forces their positions to coincide, the result is precisely a four-scalar contact vertex.

p.src: Supersymmetry has done more than place a boson and a fermion in the same theory. It has forced their masses to agree, tied the Yukawa coupling to $g$, and fixed the quartic scalar coupling to $|g|^2$. These relations could be tested through masses, scattering amplitudes, and decays; they are not optional numerical coincidences.

p.src: Paired Loop Effects

u.src: Paired Loop Effects
en: Paired Loop Effects

p.src: The relations become most useful when interactions correct particle masses. The scalar self-energy receives a bosonic loop from the quartic vertex and a fermionic loop from two Yukawa vertices. Each carries two powers of the same coupling. A closed fermion loop has the relative minus sign required by Fermi statistics.

p.src: At one loop the leading ultraviolet-sensitive pieces cancel between the complete bosonic and fermionic contributions. The same symmetry organizes higher orders through Ward identities and nonrenormalization properties. The statement concerns symmetry-related sums, not a literal one-to-one cancellation of every graph; wave-function renormalization, finite effects, and other symmetry-preserving corrections can remain. This is the practical power of building the theory in superspace: the equality of masses and the relations among couplings are enforced before any individual Feynman integral is evaluated.

p.src: The model constructed here is the simplest interacting chiral theory, commonly called the Wess–Zumino model. It is an example, not the most general supersymmetric field theory, but the pattern persists: represent fields by supermultiplets, write invariant superspace integrals, and let the Grassmann expansion enforce component relations.

p.src: Exact supersymmetry is not visible in the observed particle spectrum, so the next problem is how the symmetry can be broken while retaining enough of its ultraviolet control to be useful. The other promised direction is grand unification: how $SU(3)\times SU(2)\times U(1)$ may fit into a larger group such as $SU(5)$, and how supersymmetric particle content changes that unification story. Those are the questions to which the remaining lectures turn.
